definition: A standard Roblox VFX construction pattern: build one visual effect (here, fire) from TWO independently-configured `ParticleEmitter`s on separate attachments rather than one — an inner 'core' (a flipbook-mode animated sprite texture, near-zero Speed so particles barely travel, short fixed Lifetime, low Rate, high Brightness/LightEmission, a tight bright-to-dark color gradient) layered with an outer 'glow' (ordinary drifting particles, larger Size, longer/randomized Lifetime, higher Rate, lower LightEmission, transparency fading out over life, some rotation) — each emitter tuned as a distinct sub-element of one composite effect rather than one emitter doing everything.
purpose: Get a more convincing result than a single emitter can produce, by splitting a visual effect's distinct visual roles (a sharp, animated, bright core vs. a soft, drifting, fading ambient glow) onto separately-tunable emitters rather than compromising on one emitter's settings to try to do both jobs at once.
visible_effect: A single-emitter fire reads as either too sharp/mechanical (if tuned for the crisp flipbook look alone) or too soft/shapeless (if tuned for the drifting glow alone); the two-layer composite reads as a small bright animated flame core sitting inside a larger soft ambient glow, closer to a real fire's own layered visual structure.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: Not applicable beyond the visual result itself — a more convincing, less 'placeholder-looking' effect reads as more polished/intentional, the source's own stated goal ('make your effects really pop or look way better').
physical_interpretation: Loosely mimics a real fire's own layered structure (a sharp inner flame silhouette within a softer outer heat/glow radius), though the source is explicit this is an artistic approximation via two particle streams, not a physical simulation.
use_cases: any VFX (fire, magic, energy, impact) where a single emitter's settings cannot simultaneously serve both a sharp defining silhouette and a soft ambient spread, and splitting the roles onto two emitters gives each the freedom to be tuned for its own job

specifically pairing a flipbook-textured (animated-sprite) core with ordinary procedural-particle glow, when a hand-drawn/pre-rendered animated texture reads better for a defining shape than procedural particles alone would
non_use_cases: a simple, small, or distant effect where a single emitter's result is already good enough and the added authoring/tuning cost of a second layer is not worth it
an effect with no need for a sharp defining element at all (pure ambient glow/mist effects, where one softer emitter alone may be the whole intended look)
interactions: arc_trail_vfx_readability (merged, W01) — a sibling case of VFX doing representational work (there: readability of a fast motion; here: convincing a static/ambient effect) via a compositional choice rather than a single parameter tweak

VFXSPEC_LIMITATIONS' own stated boundary (see cadence_representation) — this entry is a concrete, real-world example of exactly the class of effect that boundary already names as out of scope for the simpler path
cadence_representation: Checked directly against this build's own VFX architecture rather than assumed: Cadence has TWO VFX systems, and this technique lands differently on each. `ai/vfxspec.js` compiles a declarative spec onto a SINGLE `kind:'vfx'` emitter item, and its own top-of-file documentation states directly that it 'cannot author a multi-layer PNX effect, and does not pretend to' — this video's two-emitter composite is exactly that excluded case for the simple path. `particleLibrary.js`'s existing 'fire' material archetype (used by both the Inspector and VFX Studio) confirms this concretely: it is ONE single-layer entry (`shape:'glow', motion:'rise', blend:'additive', colorStart:'#ffd36b', colorEnd:'#7a1400', lifetime:[0.5,1.0], rate:45`, no flipbook field at all) — a reasonable single-emitter approximation, not the two-layer composite this video builds. The full procedural PNX engine (`renderer/js/pnx/**`, 390+ node types) DOES have flipbook/texture-sequence support (confirmed present in `pnx/nodes/texture.js`, `pnx/render.js` and others) and can compose multiple layers, making it — not VFXSpec — the right tool in this build for reproducing this exact technique faithfully.
control_surface: `vfx_new_effect`/`vfx_add_layer`/`vfx_apply_preset` (the simpler emitter-item path) versus the PNX tools (`pnx_add_node`, `pnx_add_recipe`, etc.) for the full multi-layer/flipbook version; no existing preset in `particleLibrary.js` currently offers this specific two-layer core+glow fire composite.
detection_and_measurement_methods: Not a motion measurement — a VFX-authoring compositional pattern. `vfx_validate`/`pnx_verify` could in principle check a built effect's layer count and per-layer texture-mode against this pattern, but no such check exists today.
generation_or_modification_methods: `particleLibrary.js`'s single-layer 'fire' archetype could be extended with a genuine two-layer core+glow variant using this build's own PNX layering (not the simpler VFXSpec path, per the boundary above); not implemented in this build today.
failure_modes: attempting this exact composite through `vfxspec.js`/the single emitter-item path, which its own documented limitation already rules out for a genuinely multi-layer effect
using only one emitter and compromising between a sharp core look and a soft glow look, producing a result weaker than either role tuned independently
roblox_considerations: Built entirely from native Roblox `ParticleEmitter` properties (Brightness/LightEmission, Color, Size, Texture, Transparency, ZOffset, Lifetime, Rate, Speed, SpreadAngle, and flipbook-mode texture animation) attached to two separate `Attachment`s — a standard, broadly-applicable Roblox VFX construction pattern, not specific to fire or to this source's own plugins.
performance_implications: Two active emitters cost roughly twice the particle simulation/render load of one; a reasonable trade for the visual improvement in most cases, but worth being deliberate about for effects that will be instantiated many times at once (e.g. many simultaneous player-triggered effects).
examples: the inner 'core' emitter: a 4x4 flipbook texture in 'one shot' mode, LightEmission ~0.8, Brightness 5, a bright-orange-to-darker color gradient, Lifetime 0.5s, Rate 2, Speed 0.001 (deliberately near-zero so particles barely travel), a modest spread angle (video @ 04:41–05:45)

the outer 'glow' emitter: duplicated from the core then retuned — lower LightEmission, a darker color, transparency fading out over the particle's life, randomized/longer Lifetime, higher Rate, larger Size, added rotation (video @ 05:49–06:20, confirmed in this session's own earlier frames showing the property-explainer sequence for Spread Angle and related properties, t=04:35)
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/xzZeP65SSlA @ 04:41–06:20 — Stoic (the presenter) builds and narrates the full two-layer construction live, naming every property and value directly; Cadence's own `vfxspec.js` boundary documentation, `particleLibrary.js`'s single-layer fire archetype, and the PNX engine's flipbook support were all read directly in this session (not assumed) to ground the cadence_representation comparison; experimental until validated
